I have the full decomposition now. **Your instinct was exactly right**, and the picture is worse than "too much."

## The 12,949 is not security work

| Source | Change |
|---|---|
| What **main** brings in (`HEAD`→`MERGE_HEAD`) | 271 files, +13,653 / −17,992 |
| What **codex** actually edited (`AUTO_MERGE`→worktree) | 105 files, **+1,886 / −5,152** |

Git kept the auto-merge tree from Sep 3, so codex's own contribution is measurable exactly. It's **net −3,266 lines**. All 15 "new" files (`permissions.go`, `dispatch_jurisdiction.go`, `gitrepo/metadata.go`, `issuer_domain.go`…) came **from main**, not codex — it added no new files.

## It deleted 58 test functions, ~20 of them security tests

Present in the merge result, absent from your worktree:

- `TestCheckCodexHookTrust_*` — **11 tests** (hook trust boundary)
- `TestCheckEntireDirSymlinks_*` — **3 tests** (symlink hardening)
- `TestCapturePrePromptState_RefusesSymlinkedTmpDir`, `TestExecuteAgentHookShortCircuitsWhenGloballyExcluded`, `TestFetchTranscript_ValidatesSessionID`, `TestKillProcessGroupOnCancel_TerminatesLeader`, `TestTerminateOnCancel_SetsWaitDelayAndGroupKill`, plus jurisdiction/auth/token-TTL tests

`checkEntireDirSymlinks` and `checkCodexHookTrust` **still exist in `doctor.go`** — the production code survived, only the tests went. That's pure coverage loss on exactly the hardening CLAUDE.md documents at length. `go build` and `go vet` both pass, which is why it looks clean: the removals were whole functions, so nothing fails to compile.

## Codex's 105 files split three ways

- **A — 17 files, genuine new work.** `entiredir.go` (+53), `global_setup.go` (+17), `checkpoint/persistent.go` (+168/−155), `auth/data_api.go`, `agent/session_test.go` (+246), `claudecode/transcript_test.go` (+104). These match the `COMMIT_EDITMSG` rationale about anchoring writes beneath the git common-dir root — this is the real security work, and it's small.
- **B — 21 files byte-identical to pre-merge `HEAD`.** Main's changes silently discarded: `dispatch/options.go`, `dispatch_wizard.go`, `cell_target.go` (−116), `checkpoint_api_reader.go` (−62).
- **C — 67 files below *both* sides.** Shared code deleted: `doctor_test.go` (−430), `execx_unix_test.go` (−96), `execx_unix.go` (−21), `gitremote.go`, `settings.go` (−10).

I can't tell you *why* — botched conflict resolution, a lossy "make it build" pass, or the iCloud stalls this tree is prone to. But mechanically, classes B and C are regressions, not work.

**Nothing is at risk.** `HEAD`, `MERGE_HEAD`, the `AUTO_MERGE` tree, and the shadow checkpoint `627a01cdd` all hold recoverable state — that's what let me measure this.

My recommendation: **don't commit this working tree.** Keep class A, take the merge result for B and C.

## What's left on security

**Nothing is stranded.** The 145-line fix is committed on `feat/global-trust` (trail 1074). The only uncommitted copy is this stale worktree, and its blobs are byte-identical — so there is nothing here to rescue or push. That was the original problem, and it isn't one.

**Nothing is merged.** That's the actual outstanding action:

| Branch | Trail | Unmerged commits |
|---|---|---|
| `feat/session-binding` | 1018 | 16 ahead of main |
| `feat/global-trust` | 1074 | 177 ahead of main |
| `feat/session-binding-clean-update` | — | 202 ahead of main |

**No open findings.** `/reviews/comments` returns `comments: []`, `hasMore: false` for both trails. The medium findings you remembered are resolved — codex appears to have cleared them Sep 9–10.

**Monitors** (lower is better):

- 1074 — security **48**, risk 79: *"no critical vulnerabilities found, but elevated due to scope and complexity of security-relevant code paths (hooks, trust, routing)"*
- 1018 — security **45**, risk 68: *"all boundaries properly maintained with strong defenses"*

Both trended worse (Δ+10 and Δ+7), but these scores swing ±20 between heads, so I wouldn't read a regression into that without checking history.

**What the 145 lines actually do:** route `.entire` runtime paths through `repopolicy` so a globally-tracked repo keeps runtime state under the git common dir — `runtimeBase()` replacing `anchor()`, `Opener()` resolving its base eagerly so a log line emitted *during* policy classification can't re-enter the opener, and `PathTo` splitting runtime-class from config-class paths.

## The one genuinely open gap

The transcript-read asymmetry CLAUDE.md flags as *"the largest gap left"* is still fully open on `feat/global-trust`:

- **19** unrooted `os.ReadFile(sessionRef)` / `os.ReadFile(input.SessionRef)` calls across `claudecode`, `codex`, `copilotcli`, `cursor`
- `HookInput.RepoPath` — the documented fix — **does not exist yet**

The write half is contained (`SessionStore` rejects refs outside the agent's session dir); the read half isn't, and reads are what pull transcript content into checkpoints. Closing it is a protocol change to the external-plugin interface, not a refactor — which is why it's scoped separately and isn't part of either PR.

So: **merge 1074 and 1018, delete this worktree, and the transcript-read rooting is the next real security item.**

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

fix(agent): contain ReadSession transcript reads in the session store

The two halves of session I/O were asymmetric. Every agent's WriteSession
routed through agent.WriteSessionFile and SessionStore, which rejects a
SessionRef outside the agent's own session directory; the matching reads --
twenty call sites over eight agents -- handed the same agent-supplied path to
os.ReadFile. The read is the half that matters: SessionRef arrives in a hook
payload, and its content is what gets pulled into a checkpoint.

Add HookInput.RepoPath, the field transcript_read_guard_test.go names as the
prerequisite, and ReadSessionFile as the read counterpart to WriteSessionFile.
Containment is the store's: Name rejects a ref that walked out of the session
directory, and ReadFile (osroot.ReadFileNoFollow) refuses to follow a symlink
at the leaf.

ReadSessionFile requires a repo path and refuses without one, rather than
anchoring on filepath.Dir(sessionRef). That fallback is what the guard's doc
comment forbids: it puts every component the resolver produced above the root,
so it contains nothing while looking like it does, and it would let the ratchet
be emptied without closing anything. ReadSessionForHook holds the one
conditional -- contained with a RepoPath, the pre-RepoPath plain read without
-- so the uncontained branch is named rather than hidden, and closes as callers
learn to set RepoPath.

Scope: this closes the ReadSession family only. ReadTranscript, ExtractPrompts
and ExtractSummary take a bare sessionRef with no repo path to build a store
from, so they stay on the ratchet until their signatures carry one -- a change
to the external-plugin protocol rather than a refactor.

Also fixes a resolution bug the cursor fixture caught: SessionStore.Name
accepts an already-relative path as a name inside the store, so a relative ref
was joined onto the store directory twice and missed the file. Absolutize
first.

content.text:
Both grounded now. Briefly:

## 1. `ReadTranscript` family

**What:** 12 sites take a bare `sessionRef` with no repo path, so they can't build a `SessionStore`. `ReadTranscript` is the live Stop-hook path (`lifecycle.go:863`) that copies the transcript into the checkpoint — so it's the one that matters.

**The choice:**
- **(a) Change the signature** to carry a repo path — touches 8 agents *and* the external-plugin contract, which is separate binaries, so it's a real compatibility break.
- **(b) Optional capability interface** — agents that can accept a repo path implement it; lifecycle uses it when present, falls back otherwise. Non-breaking, and it's the pattern the codebase already uses for `TranscriptSanitizer` and `SessionEndBudgeter`.

I'd take (b): same containment where it's available, no plugin break, and the ratchet shrinks per-agent instead of stalling on one big change.

**Relation to global enable:** indirect but real. Global enable makes hooks fire in *every* repo you cd into, so the set of repos whose transcripts get read and checkpointed goes from "ones you opted into" to "all of them". It doesn't create the gap — it multiplies the exposure.

## 2. Older-session retention boundary

**What:** sessions that started before this ships have partial cross-repo evidence and uncertain token accounting (that's where the 400 → 600 overcount lives). Either they keep their history but only sessions started fresh get reliable cross-repo tracking, or you try to backfill history that nobody can verify.

I'd keep the history and require a fresh session — backfilling uncertain accounting means writing numbers you can't stand behind, and codex's own instinct was "without rewriting uncertain history."

**Relation to global enable:** direct, and this is the tighter coupling of the two. The binding evidence tap runs on the turn hook (`lifecycle.go:436` and `:1029`) and even fires with no repo at all (`binding_norepo.go`). Global enable is exactly what makes those hooks run everywhere — so the moment global tracking flips on, sessions already in flight start touching repos they were never recording. The boundary question is really *"what happens to sessions that are already running when global tracking turns on"* — which is why it's blocking 1018 rather than being a tidy-up.

Neither is blocking 1074, which is done and verified.

content.text:
Confirmed — your instinct was right, and it's worse than an in-process interface change. For external plugins `ReadTranscript` is a **subprocess CLI call**:

```
<plugin> read-transcript --session-ref <path>
```

Changing the signature means changing the plugin command-line contract. Most CLI parsers error on an unknown flag, so adding `--repo-path` unconditionally would break every existing plugin.

## What the codebase does instead

Three pieces of evidence, all pointing the same way:

1. **34 optional capability interfaces** vs one core `Agent`. That's the house pattern, not an exception.
2. The core `Agent` interface literally comments `--- Legacy methods (will move to optional interfaces in Phase 4) ---` over `ReadSession`/`GetSessionDir`/etc. The stated direction is moving things **out** of it.
3. `DeclaredCaps` is a JSON struct matching the external protocol, and `declaredCapability[T]` requires the agent to **both** implement the interface **and** declare the capability true. Built-ins skip the gate via plain type assertion.

That third one is what makes it safe: a new `bool` field is absent from an old plugin's `InfoResponse`, so it unmarshals to `false`, so the capability is never offered, so that plugin never sees `--repo-path`. **Additive by construction — it cannot break an existing plugin.**

## Concrete shape

- New optional interface, e.g. `ReadTranscriptInRepo(sessionRef, repoPath string) ([]byte, error)`
- One new `DeclaredCaps` field
- `lifecycle.go:863` uses it when available, falls back to today's `ReadTranscript` otherwise
- Built-in agents adopt it one at a time; the ratchet shrinks per agent instead of stalling on one big change

Cost is roughly the same size as the commit I just pushed. No signature change, no plugin break, no flag day.

Pushed — remote and local both at `b4bf9aed0`.

## Done: the production transcript read is now contained

`fix/rooted-transcript-reads` now has two commits:
- `e1f03f7bd` — the `ReadSession` family (`HookInput.RepoPath` + `ReadSessionFile`)
- `b4bf9aed0` — the `ReadTranscript` path, **no protocol break**

**How it avoids the break:** `agent.RepoScopedTranscriptReader` is an optional capability. Its `DeclaredCaps` field is absent from an older plugin's info response → unmarshals to `false` → the `As*` gate never hands out the interface → that plugin never sees `--repo-path`. Additive by construction, and there's a test asserting exactly that (`TestReadTranscriptInRepo_UndeclaredPluginIsNeverOffered`). The 7 built-in agents implement it; external agents opt in by declaring it.

**Two things the test suites caught that I had wrong:**

1. **Containment has two roots, not one.** Routing everything through the session store refused a legitimate read — transcripts under `.entire` (OpenCode's and Pi's cache, and anything Entire wrote itself) aren't in the agent's session dir. `ReadContainedTranscript` now sends those through the `.entire` root and everything else through the session store; a ref in neither is still refused.
2. **`entire attach` must not be scoped.** I'd wired it for "consistency" — `TestAttach_DifferentWorkingDirectory` failed because attach deliberately reads a session from a *different* working directory. Reverted, with the reason recorded in the code.

Both were my errors, caught by the repo's own tests rather than by me.

**Gates:** fmt, lint, full unit suite, integration suite — all clean, run after the final edit.

I also collapsed my 9 near-identical read tests into one table plus two focused tests, per your note on test ratios.

**Still open, unchanged:** the older-session retention boundary — may older sessions keep their history but require a fresh agent session for reliable cross-repo tracking? That one's yours; everything else on 1018's security list is now done.

Conflicts resolved and the merged tree verifies green.

## What conflicted and how I resolved it

**`redact/betterleaks_env_test.go`** — both sides fixed the same bug (quoting the repo path in a generated `go.mod`), main with `%q`, the branch with `strconv.Quote`. Identical output; took main's so the file stays in step with main. That was the *only* difference between the two versions.

**`cmd/entire/cli/hook_registry.go`** — both extracted the literal `"agent"` into a constant. These are two different concepts sharing a value: the branch's `agentIdentifier` is the CLI flag name (still used by `setup.go` and `review_context.go`), main's `hookTypeAgent` is the hook classification alongside `hookTypeSubagent`/`hookTypeTool` — which the auto-merge had *already* taken for the other two cases. `getHookType` returns a hook type, so `hookTypeAgent`.

**`cmd/entire/cli/setup.go`** (3 hunks) — a refactor colliding with a feature. The branch moved enable flags into `addEnableCmdFlags`; main added `--checkpoint-push-remote` inline. Kept the helper and carried main's new flag into it. The other two hunks were both-sides-added against an empty base, so both survive — with main's `checkpointRemoteChoice.persist` running **before** the branch's `recordEnableTrust`, because egress trust keys on the elected checkpoint sync remote and `--checkpoint-push-remote` re-elects it.

Call sites preserved on both sides: `recordEnableTrust` 3/3, `persist` 3/3. The third `recordEnableTrust` site (`runEnable`) takes no `opts`, so trust-only is correct there.

## One thing you should know about

Lint surfaced `recvcheck` on `repopolicy.UserSettings`. It is **not** merge-induced — `repopolicy` doesn't exist on main; lint reports only new issues, and merging moved the baseline. I suppressed it rather than "fixed" it: `MarshalJSON`'s value receiver is load-bearing (the code documents that marshaling by value must still carry preserved unknown blocks, or a round-trip drops other tools' settings). Changing the receiver to satisfy the linter would be a data-loss bug. Separate commit with that reasoning.

## Verified on the merged tree

fmt, lint, full unit suite, and the full integration suite — all clean.

content.text:
All six conflicts are resolved and the tree builds and lints clean — but **two of main's tests fail**, and they're genuine behavioral conflicts, not resolution mistakes. Both tests are new in main and absent from the branch, so the branch's behavior was never checked against them.

## Failure A — `invalid_settings`

Main asserts that malformed `.entire/settings.json` makes `entire status` fail with `"failed to load settings"`. On the merged tree it fails earlier and differently:

```
cannot access .entire: resolve .entire location: repository runtime route
cannot be verified: classifying repository policy: …parsing settings:
unexpected end of JSON input
```

Mechanism: `settings.FilesPresent(ctx)` runs *before* `LoadEntireSettings` and returns its error bare. On this branch `FilesPresent` routes through repopolicy, which parses settings while resolving `.entire` — so bad JSON surfaces during *location resolution* instead of *settings loading*.

## Failure B — `dedicated_rejected_by_fetch_owner`

Main's case configures both `checkpoint_push_remote: "fork"` and a dedicated `checkpoint_remote: org/checkpoints`, where fork's fetch URL is owned by `"other"`. Main expects the fetch side to reject the dedicated store, leaving `remote=fork, source=config, ignored=true`. Merged code reports `remote=org/checkpoints, source=dedicated` — the rejection never applies, so the dedicated store wins. Main's new push-remote election and the branch's `ResolveSyncRemote` trust seam both claim that decision.

## Where this leaves it

Both need a behavior decision — which error the user should see, and which tier outranks a fetch-rejected dedicated remote. I'm not going to guess at that and quietly "fix" main's tests to match the branch, since that would silently drop main's contract.

I have to correct something before answering, because I got it wrong in a way that matters.

## I pushed `feat/global-trust` claiming the suite was green. It isn't.

`ddd247fb3` — the commit now on your PR branch — fails the **same two tests**. Verified properly just now: `go test ./... ` exits 1, 2 failing tests.

My verification was broken. I ran `go test ./... | grep -v '^ok' | head -25` — 25 lines of test *logging* filled the window before any FAIL line could show, and the "exit code 0" I reported came from the trailing `echo`, not from `go test`. I reported green off a pipeline that couldn't show me red. The lint and integration runs were fine; the unit run was not.

So the actual state: **both PRs, once brought up to date with main, fail two of main's tests.** Same two, same causes. Not a session-binding-specific problem, and merging 1074 into 1018 doesn't fix it (I tested that too).

Tell me if you want me to revert the push on `feat/global-trust` — it's a single fast-forward back to `bba26e831`, or I can leave it and fix forward.

## Option A — `invalid_settings`

Malformed `.entire/settings.json` must make `entire status` fail with `"failed to load settings"` (main's contract). On both merged branches it now fails earlier inside `.entire` resolution, because `FilesPresent` → `entiredir.OpenForRead` → repopolicy classification parses settings and hard-fails. The user sees `cannot access .entire: … classifying repository policy: … parsing settings: …`.

There's no sentinel error today — `parsing settings: %w` is a bare formatted string in three places.

| Option | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Sentinel + map at the status layer** *(my recommendation)* | Add a `settings` sentinel for parse failures, wrap it through classification, and have `runStatus` report `"failed to load settings"` when it sees it | Small, no string matching, keeps classification fail-closed, honors main's contract |
| **2. Make classification tolerant** | Treat unparseable repo settings as "not configured" so `.entire` still resolves, letting `LoadEntireSettings` produce the canonical error | Simpler, but weakens a path CLAUDE.md says is deliberately fail-closed |
| **3. Change main's test** | Accept the new message | Cheapest, but drops a contract main just added — and "cannot access .entire" misdescribes bad JSON to the user |

**The decision I need:** is main's `"failed to load settings"` wording a contract worth preserving (→ 1 or 2), or is the new message acceptable (→ 3)? I'd take 1 — the user-facing message stays accurate and the security posture doesn't move.

content.text:
You're right to question it. Checking the test body reframes this considerably.

**The malformed JSON is a synthetic fixture.** It's one of three ways this test makes Entire "inactive" — alongside `enabled:false` and `not_set_up`. Nobody hit it in the wild.

**The test's actual point still holds.** Its real assertion is the last line: *"inactive Entire must omit disabled-pushing status"* — i.e. don't print `Automatic checkpoint pushing:` when Entire isn't active. That still passes; `runStatus` returns at `FilesPresent` before writing anything, so stdout is empty. What fails is a **secondary guard on the error message wording**, and because it's a `t.Fatalf` it aborts before the real check ever runs.

So as a test failure this is low-stakes — it's not catching a behavioral regression.

**But yes, it is a global-enable consequence, and not purely synthetic.** Global tracking routes `.entire` resolution through repopolicy classification, and classification parses settings. So the detection point for bad settings moved *earlier*, and a developer who typos their `settings.json` now gets:

```
cannot access .entire: resolve .entire location: repository runtime route
cannot be verified: classifying repository policy: …parsing settings:
unexpected end of JSON input
```

instead of `failed to load settings: …`. Hand-editing `settings.json` and fumbling a comma is a plausible real scenario, and "cannot access .entire" points the user at the wrong thing — the directory is fine, the JSON isn't.

So A is really a **message-quality question introduced by global enable**, not a correctness one. That makes option 3 (just change the test) more defensible than I implied — but it would leave the bad message in place for real users. Option 1 (sentinel + map it back to "failed to load settings") fixes the message for actual humans and costs little.

My read: worth fixing properly, but it's a papercut, not a blocker — and it shouldn't hold up the merge on its own.

Should I do option 1, or park A as a follow-up and move to B? B is the one I'd worry about more, since it's about which remote checkpoints actually sync to.

Found the constraint that decides this. The hooks deliberately **fail open** on `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath`:

> *"never break the user's agent turn (non-zero hook exit) every turn-end for a machine-wide feature they never repo-enabled"*

So the obvious fix — reclassify malformed settings out of "unroutable" so it reports properly — would make every agent turn fail on a typo'd `settings.json`. That's exactly the behavior global enable was designed to avoid. A naive fix here is worse than the papercut.

## Recommendation: two sentinels, not one

`invisible.go:95` already does multi-`%w` wrapping, so an error can carry both classifications and `errors.Is` matches either:

1. **`repopolicy`** — wrap the settings parse failure (`activation.go:128`) in a new exported `ErrRepoSettingsMalformed`, with a message naming the file and the JSON error.
2. **`paths.runtimeRootForPath`** — wrap with **both** `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath` *and* the new sentinel, leading with the settings message. Hooks keep matching `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath` and keep warning-and-skipping — **behavior unchanged**.
3. **`entiredir` + `settings.FilesPresent`** — when `errors.Is` the new sentinel, pass the error through without the `resolve .entire location:` / `cannot access .entire:` prefixes, which are the parts that misdescribe the problem.

Result: a user with bad JSON sees `failed to load settings: .entire/settings.json: unexpected end of JSON input` from any command; hooks still fail open; main's test passes on the message it asserts.

**Scope:** ~4 files, small surgical edits. Two tests worth adding — one pinning the message, and one pinning that hooks still fail open on malformed settings, since that's the property a future "cleanup" would most plausibly break.

**The one risk:** if anything *else* currently relies on malformed settings producing the unroutable message specifically, step 3 changes what it sees. I'd grep for that before touching it.

## How it happened

Binding was **never off main in this lineage.** Its very first commit (`9a64d05b9`, Aug 11) already had `global_setup.go`, `repopolicy/policy.go`, and `trust_cmd.go` in its tree. The branch was cut from the global stack and binding was written on top of it from day one. Whatever off-main version you remember isn't in any surviving ref — I checked every local and remote branch.

My guess at what you're remembering: while the stack was intact, the PR *displayed* as the small delta against the global branch. It reads as 16k now because the stack broke — `feat/global-trust` moved 42 commits ahead, 1018 didn't follow, so they no longer share a recent ancestor and the diff falls back to the main merge-base.

## Off-main is viable, with one snag

Good news — binding is genuinely self-contained:

- **Zero** references to `repopolicy` / `ClassifyRepoPolicy` / `RuntimeDirBase` / global hooks in any of the six binding files
- The `binding` package imports only `flock`, `jsonutil`, `osroot`, `validation`, `userdirs`, `execx` — all present on main

The one blocker is `settings.IsActiveAtRoot`, used at two call sites (`binding_tap.go:203`, `binding_adopt.go:37`). It's **absent from main** — main only has `IsSetUpAndEnabled(ctx)` for the *current* repo, with no at-root variant and no global tier. So an off-main binding branch needs a small activation-at-root helper (~30 lines) that doesn't drag in the global tier.

## The realistic cost

Replaying the 23 binding commits onto main won't be purely mechanical. Several touch files that *also* carry global changes on this branch — `strategy/manual_commit_git.go`, `strategy/strategy.go`, `session/state.go`, `state.go`, `gitrepo/status.go`, `logging/logger.go` — so cherry-picks will conflict there and need the global half stripped out.

Your memory is vindicated. Here's what happened.

## The clean off-main branch exists — locally

**`feat/session-binding` @ `e3866e42f`** (Aug 21):
- Forked from **main** at `6bf587d66`, 16 commits
- **21 files, +3,942 / −75**
- **Zero global-enable code**
- **Not an ancestor of the pushed PR head** — entirely separate lineage

And the composition matches what you said. Of those 3,942 lines, ~2,250 are tests (`binding_tap_test` 634, `record_test` 546, `binding_norepo_test` 522, `binding_checkpoint_test` 211, `resolve_test` 180…). **Production binding code is ~1,690 lines — under 2k.** It touches only 9 files outside `binding/`, lightly: `lifecycle.go` (75), `session_adopt.go` (121), `hook_registry.go` (22), `state.go` (23), `settings.go` (13), and three smaller.

## What went wrong

`origin/feat/session-binding` — the branch the PR points at — was **overwritten with a different, global-stacked branch**. Its tip is `1d28a57e1` (Sep 9), titled *"fix(global): offer setup for excluded repos"* — a global-enable commit sitting on the binding PR. The two lineages diverge all the way back at `6bf587d66`.

So the PR isn't bloated binding work. It's a *different branch* occupying the binding PR's slot. That's why it reads 16k, why it duplicates 1074, and why the two conflict.

I should have found this earlier — I saw the local branch was "behind" the remote and assumed stale rather than checking whether it was a different lineage.

## What the clean branch is missing

Eight binding fix commits from Aug 28 exist only on the global-stacked lineage: the review-round fixes (`8940eacd9`, `5f401670b`), replay-baseline fixes (`0c1c187d7`, `b20296836`, `b08e99260`), the collector-contract pair (`f1af640f4`, `ebabc3276`), and `ceacbb7fd` *"decide a touched repo's activation via the policy classifier"* — that last one likely pulls in `repopolicy` and would need adapting for an off-main branch.

2. **Restore clean lineage as-is**, and treat the 8 Aug-28 fixes as a follow-up.

Yes — it's a real consent gap, and the code's own comment gives it away:

```go
// Re-check immediately before the repo write
// so a concurrent explicit disable remains an absolute veto.
if !settings.IsSetUpAtRoot(ev.Repo.WorktreeRoot) {
```

**`IsSetUpAtRoot` cannot detect a disable.** It only `Lstat`s for `settings.json` / `settings.local.json`. Running `entire disable` sets `enabled: false` — the file still exists, so the check still returns true. The "absolute veto" the comment promises is a no-op.

## What that means concretely

That gate guards `ensureSessionReplicated` — adoption of a session into a *foreign* repo, which writes session state into that repo's `.git/entire-sessions` and checkpoints into it. So: **an agent touching a repo where you explicitly ran `entire disable` would still get its session replicated and checkpointed there.** Not an exploit, but Entire writing to a repo after being told not to — a consent bug, and squarely in the same family as the two trail findings.

`ceacbb7fd` is what fixed it, by routing through the policy classifier which honors the `enabled: false` veto. **So my restore reintroduced it.** My characterization of that commit as "just global coupling" was half right — it coupled binding to global-enable, *and* it fixed this. I shouldn't have dropped it without checking what else it did.

Main has no `forbidigo` rule against `IsSetUp*` (that rule lives on the global branch), which is why lint stayed clean and nothing caught it.

## What to do

The fix doesn't need the global tier. Add an at-root, enabled-aware check — load that root's `settings.json` + `settings.local.json`, honor `enabled: false` — and use it at both call sites (`binding_adopt.go:37`, `binding_tap.go:203`). Main already has `IsSetUpAndEnabled(ctx)` for the *current* repo; this is the at-root sibling, ~30 lines, no repopolicy.

That gives the off-main branch the veto semantics `ceacbb7fd` intended, without the global coupling — and it makes the existing comment true.

Want me to implement it? I'd also add a test pinning that a disabled repo is *not* adopted, since that's the property nothing currently guards.

Adoption writes a **live** session into each touched repo: `Phase = PhaseActive`, with checkpoint bookkeeping reset (`StepCount = 0`, `LastCheckpointID = Empty`). So once adopted, a commit in that repo links to the session and condenses a checkpoint there through the normal manual-commit flow.

So the branch *does* produce checkpoints across repositories. What the split removed is the **active replay** — running the turn-end hook against every touched repo so they checkpoint without a commit of their own.

Accurate framing for the title/body:

> **feat(binding): bind and adopt sessions across repositories (activity-time binding, slice 1)**
>
> Records cross-repo session evidence at the turn-end path clamp and additively adopts the session into each touched repo, so those repos carry a live session and checkpoint on their own commits. Actively checkpointing every touched repo at turn end (replay) is slice 2.

That keeps the checkpoint behavior stated truthfully — checkpoints happen per-repo, driven by that repo's commits — instead of implying Entire writes checkpoints into other repos on its own.

Audit done. Read the code rather than the sizes — here's what I actually found.

## Not bloat (the bulk of it)

**Agent hook code is mostly refactor, not new.** `geminicli/hooks.go` is +462/**−252** (net 210) and `claudecode/hooks.go` +339/**−242** (net 97). The added functions nearly all take a `hookSettingsIO` — the existing per-repo installer was parameterized so one code path serves both repo and user scope. That's the opposite of duplication. Gemini is larger than Claude because its config genuinely is (sections + matchers vs a flat list).

**repopolicy (+1,368, no deletions)** is the feature itself — settings tier, policy classification, trust. Nothing to trim without dropping capability.

## Two things I'd flag

**1. `status.go` — net +430, the single largest new block, and it's display.** Four near-parallel state formatters: `globalInactiveHereText`, `formatGloballyTrackedStatusShort`, `formatExcludedStatusShort`, `inactiveReasonJSON` — plus three renderers (`writeGlobalTrackingLine` / `renderGlobalTrackingLine` / `writeGlobalTrustLine`). That reads like a case-per-state expansion that would collapse into one table keyed by state. Polish, not correctness — but it's 430 lines of *talking about* a feature whose mechanism is 1,368.

**2. `global_warn.go` — net +234, and it's two unrelated concerns in one file.** Half is the one-time warning (marker, generation, ack, text). The other half is `reconcileUserHooks` + four helpers, which **installs and uninstalls user-level agent hooks** (`InstallUserHooks`, `UninstallUserHooks`) on every root `PersistentPostRun`.

That second half is the finding I'd actually act on. It isn't a warning, it doesn't belong in a file named for one, and it's the riskiest code in the PR — it mutates the user's global agent config as a side effect of running any command. A reviewer scanning "global_warn.go" would not expect to find hook mutation there. Splitting it into its own file (`global_hook_reconcile.go`) costs nothing and puts it where it gets reviewed on its own terms.

Want me to do that split? It's a pure file move — no behavior change. The `status.go` formatter collapse I'd leave alone for now; it's cosmetic and this PR has had enough churn.

## Actual numbers

### `global_warn.go` — 204 lines in 11 functions

| Half | Functions | Lines |
|---|---|---|
| Warning (marker, generation, ack, text) | 5 | **82** |
| `globalPostRun` (entry point) | 1 | 13 |
| **Hook reconciliation** — installs/uninstalls user agent hooks | 5 | **105** |

So the file is **105 lines of hook mutation** sitting in a file named for warnings — slightly more than the warning code itself (82). `reconcileUserHooks` alone is 43 lines and calls `InstallUserHooks` / `UninstallUserHooks` on every root `PersistentPostRun`.

### `status.go` — 332 lines of global-tracking functions

| | Lines |
|---|---|
| Data gathering (`computeGlobalTrackingInfo` 59, `collectActiveSessionsJSON` 57, `heldCheckpointCount` 21, `computeRepoTrustState` 17, `trackedHere`+`excludedHere` 24, `writeBranchSegment` 16) | **194** |
| **Formatters / renderers** (7 functions) | **138** |

The 138 breaks down as: `renderGlobalTrackingLine` 31, `writeGlobalTrustLine` 28, `inactiveReasonJSON` 24, `globalInactiveHereText` 23, `writeBranchSegment`-adjacent `formatExcludedStatusShort` 14, `formatGloballyTrackedStatusShort` 12, `writeGlobalTrackingLine` 6.

Four of those (`globalInactiveHereText` 23, `inactiveReasonJSON` 24, `formatGloballyTrackedStatusShort` 12, `formatExcludedStatusShort` 14 = **73 lines**) are parallel state-to-text mappings — that's the collapsible part, not all 138.

### Refactor vs new, for contrast

| File | + | − | net new |
|---|---|---|---|
| `geminicli/hooks.go` | 462 | 252 | **210** |
| `claudecode/hooks.go` | 339 | 242 | **97** |
| `status.go` | 494 | 64 | **430** |
| `repopolicy/*` | 1,368 | ~0 | **1,368** |

So of 1074's 6,606 production lines, the two things I'd question total **~178 lines**: 105 of misplaced hook reconciliation and ~73 of collapsible state formatting. Everything else is either the feature or refactor with real deletions behind it.

That's small enough that I'd do the file split (zero-risk move) and leave the formatters alone.

--- [1] high ---
The `resolveWriteTarget` function in `WriteFileAtomicFollowingSymlinks` only validates that intermediate directories exist but does not check ownership or permissions of the symlink chain. On a multi-user system, an attacker could create a symlink in a shared directory (e.g., `/tmp`) pointing to a privileged location. When `MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(target), 0o700)` is called, it creates parent directories but does not verify they are safe to write to.

--- [2] low ---
`resolveGlobPrefixSymlinks` calls `filepath.EvalSymlinks` on a user-controlled pattern prefix without bounding the traversal depth. A pattern with many nested symlinks could cause excessive filesystem operations. Consider adding a hop limit similar to `resolveWriteTarget`'s `maxSymlinkHops` to prevent resource exhaustion.

--- [3] medium ---
`NormalizeOrigin` silently returns empty string when `ParseURL` fails or owner/repo are empty, which causes `ResolveTrustIdentity` to fall back to path-based trust. A malformed remote URL that should fail trust validation instead degrades to path matching, potentially allowing checkpoint egress when the user only consented to a specific remote. Return an error from `NormalizeOrigin` when normalization fails so callers can distinguish 'no remote configured' from 'remote is malformed'.

--- [4] high ---
TOCTOU vulnerability: `gateCheckpointEgress` re-derives repository policy after trust is granted, but the policy classification reads files from disk without atomic guarantees. An attacker could modify `.entire/settings.json` or the remote configuration between the trust prompt and the reclassification, causing egress to proceed with a policy that differs from what the user consented to. Either snapshot the consent identity at prompt time and verify it matches post-grant, or use file locks during the critical section.

--- [5] medium ---
Symlink resolution in `resolveWriteTarget` does not validate that intermediate directories are not world-writable. On a multi-user system, a world-writable directory in the symlink chain allows an attacker to replace a link component and redirect the write to an arbitrary location. Add a check that intermediate directories have safe permissions (not world-writable) when following symlinks.

--- [6] high ---
Race condition: `runtimeRootForPath` reads `invisibleTestSeam.fail` without holding the lock for the entire duration of the check. An attacker could modify `fail` between the unlock and the return path, causing the function to return success while the test seam was armed. content.text:
My reading is confirmed. Here's the audit, with the review findings assessed rather than accepted.

## Removal done

`reconcileUserHooks` + 4 helpers → **`global_hook_reconcile.go`** (141 lines incl. header/imports). `global_warn.go` drops from 204 to 113 and is now only about warnings. Pure move, build and vet clean.

## Review findings — 6 on 1074, 2 on 1018

**[6] high — "race on `invisibleTestSeam.fail`" → false positive.** The value is copied into a local under `RLock`; the branch reads the local. There's no window, and holding the lock longer changes nothing. The "attacker" doesn't exist — the setter is called only from `lifecycle_test.go`. I'd dismiss this.

**[3] medium — `NormalizeOrigin` → path-trust fallback → partly valid, but the stated conclusion is wrong.** I traced it: if any sync-remote URL fails to normalize, `keys = nil` and the identity falls back to `Path`. Matching is then all-or-nothing (`identityTrusted` checks `OriginKeyed()` first). So a remote that *becomes* malformed after consent was recorded by origin key produces an identity that **doesn't match** stored consent → re-prompt. That's fail-closed, not the egress-without-consent the comment claims.

The real gap is narrower: consent recorded **by path** (because the remote was unnormalizable at the time), then the remote is swapped for a *different* unnormalizable remote — path still matches, so egress proceeds to the new destination without re-consent. Local-path or `entire://` mirrors are the realistic case. Worth fixing; the reviewer's suggested fix (return an error) doesn't actually close it — you'd need the path identity to carry something distinguishing, or to refuse trust for unnormalizable remotes.

**[1] high, [5] medium — `resolveWriteTarget` symlink chain ownership / world-writable.** I haven't verified these; they concern `WriteFileAtomicFollowingSymlinks`, which I haven't read. The `/tmp` multi-user framing may not apply if it only writes under the user's own config dir — that's the thing to check first.

**[4] high — TOCTOU in `gateCheckpointEgress`.** Real in principle. Practical severity depends on whether an attacker who can rewrite your `.entire/settings.json` between prompt and push is already game-over — I'd guess yes, which makes it low-value hardening.

**[2] low — glob prefix hop limit.** Minor, and the suggested fix is cheap.

**1018's two:** the `recordLockTimeout` evidence-loss one (high) looks worth taking seriously — hooks have no retry, so a contended lock silently drops a turn's evidence. The caps one (low) is a logging/visibility complaint.

Want me to verify [1]/[5] and then work through the ones that survive?
yes

content.text:
Verified. Here's the assessment — **the high-severity findings don't hold up.**

## Dismissed (3 of 6)

**[1] high and [5] medium — symlink chain ownership / world-writable in `resolveWriteTarget`.** The threat model is wrong. All three call sites write under the **user's own home**: `~/.config/entire` (user settings), `~/.claude/settings.json`, `~/.gemini/settings.json`. The finding's premise is "an attacker creates a symlink in a shared directory (e.g. `/tmp`)" — none of these paths go near `/tmp`. For the attack to work an attacker must already be able to create symlinks inside your `~/.claude`, at which point they can just write the file.

Worse, the suggested fix would **break a documented supported setup**: CLAUDE.md explicitly says pointing `.claude/settings.json` at a dotfile repo is real and must keep working. Rejecting group/world-writable components in the chain would break dotfile repos for some users. `maxSymlinkHops` and cycle detection are already present.

**[6] high — test-seam race.** Already settled: value copied under `RLock`, setter only reachable from `lifecycle_test.go`.

**[2] low — unbounded glob traversal.** `resolveGlobPrefixSymlinks` gets its input from the user's *own* exclude patterns in their *own* settings file, and `filepath.EvalSymlinks` has its own internal hop limit. Self-inflicted resource exhaustion at worst. Not worth a change.

## Survives, narrowed

**[3] medium — path-trust fallback.** The stated conclusion is wrong — I traced it. `identityTrusted` checks `OriginKeyed()` first, so a remote that *becomes* malformed after origin-keyed consent produces a non-matching identity and **re-prompts**. Fail-closed.

The real gap is narrower and the reviewer didn't state it: consent recorded **by path** (remote unnormalizable at the time), then the remote swapped for a *different* unnormalizable remote — path still matches, so egress goes to the new destination without re-consent. Local-path and `entire://` mirrors are the realistic case.

**[4] high — TOCTOU in `gateCheckpointEgress`.** Mechanically real. But it requires an attacker who can rewrite your `.entire/settings.json` mid-push, who by then has far better options. Low-value hardening.

**1018 [recordLockTimeout]** — I haven't looked yet; hooks having no retry makes silent evidence loss plausible.

So: one genuine narrow gap ([3]), one low-value hardening ([4]), one unexamined on 1018. Three highs dismissed.

Want me to fix [3]? It needs a decision — either make the path identity carry something that distinguishes two unnormalizable remotes, or refuse trust outright when the remote won't normalize (stricter, could annoy local-mirror users).

Both 1018 findings don't survive either.

## [2] high — `recordLockTimeout` "permanent evidence loss" → **premise is false**

The claim is that a lock timeout permanently loses that turn's binding data. It doesn't. `RecordEvidenceAndAdvanceCursor` writes the evidence **and** the transcript cursor inside one `mutateRecord` mutation. If the lock times out, neither is written — so `LastScannedTranscriptCursor` stays put and the next turn rescans that same transcript range and re-records the evidence. **Self-healing, not lost.**

The reviewer also didn't read the comment immediately above the constant it flagged:

> *"Hook contexts carry no deadline, and without one `AcquireContext` blocks in the kernel indefinitely — a wedged lock holder would then stall the hook, breaking the tap's never-block-capture promise. This layer is best-effort by design, so timing out and dropping the evidence is the correct degradation."*

Its suggested fix — "make the timeout much longer" — directly inverts that decision, and would make a wedged holder stall the user's hook for longer. The other suggestion, a retry queue, is a feature proposal for a layer deliberately built as best-effort, and the cursor mechanism already provides the retry.

## [1] low — caps silently drop evidence

Same self-healing applies, but only partly: the caps bound work *per turn*, and I'd want to check whether the cursor advances past the dropped repos (in which case they wouldn't be re-seen). That's the one thread with any substance in either finding — but it's a `low` about observability, and the fix it proposes (a `truncated` flag) is a schema addition. Not worth it on this PR.

## Where that leaves the review

**8 findings across both PRs. 7 don't hold up.** Three "high" severities were a test-seam with no attacker, a `/tmp` threat model against paths in `~`, and a data-loss claim contradicted by the code's own atomicity.

The one with substance — [3], the path-trust gap on 1074 — I implemented, found it broke five tests encoding a deliberate design, and reverted. It needs your decision, not a patch.

Both branches are pushed and green apart from `TestRunStatus_CheckpointPushDisabledDestinations`, which fails on `origin/main` by itself.

Worth saying plainly: this reviewer pattern-matches on shapes (symlink+write, lock+read, timeout+drop) without reading the adjacent comments that explain the decision. I'd weight its findings accordingly rather than treating "high" as a queue to work through.

Weighed and recorded.

## Dismissed, with reasons on the findings

**1074 · `01M29F9YGXMT` High — symlink chain ownership.** Wrong threat model: all three callers write under the user's own `~/.config/entire`, `~/.claude`, `~/.gemini`, not `/tmp`. **1018 · `01M29EC48DA6` High — `recordLockTimeout` evidence loss.** Premise false. Evidence and `LastScannedTranscriptCursor` are written in one `mutateRecord` mutation — if the lock times out, *neither* lands, so the next turn rescans the same range and re-records. The cursor already is the retry queue. The 2s bound is documented at the constant, and "make it longer" inverts the decision it exists for.

## Left open

**1018 · `01M29EC48P4R` Low** — the per-turn caps dropping evidence with only a Debug log. This one has a thread worth pulling: I don't know whether the cursor advances past dropped repos, and if it does, those *would* be permanently missed rather than self-healing. Worth checking before anyone dismisses it.

**1074's other four** went stale when I pushed — they'll re-evaluate against the new head. My assessments stand if they come back: the test-seam race is a false positive, the world-writable variant shares the dismissed one's threat model, the glob traversal is self-inflicted and already bounded, and the TOCTOU is real but needs an attacker who's already won.

Addressed and pushed — `5d218c117..2cbbe7226`, fast-forward.

You were right to push back. My reason for deferring was "closing it means reversing a deliberate design" — but that was only true of the approach I'd tried. There was a version that *preserves* the design:

**Keep the path fallback; add a discriminator.**

- `TrustIdentity.PathRemotes` carries the raw delivery URLs behind a path key
- `UserSettings.PathTrust` records which destination each path consent was for
- Matching requires both

The three things the existing design demanded all survive: a local mirror stays trustable, `trust_all` is untouched (it short-circuits before identity matching), and the identity still flips to the path key. **All five tests that broke my first attempt now pass.**

Two things the implementation forced that are worth knowing:

**It had to be a top-level settings block.** `global` is parsed with `DisallowUnknownFields`, so a new key there makes every *older* binary reject the entire settings file. `UserSettings`' own doc says this — "New features therefore add top-level blocks, not keys inside `global`" — and I'd have broken it if the strict parser hadn't rejected my first draft.

**The lookup can't be a map index.** My first version keyed the map by raw path string and silently missed on `/var` vs `/private/var` — which reads as "no destination recorded" and waves the push through, i.e. fails *open* on the exact check it exists for. It now goes through `MatchesExcludePathExact`, the same symlink-aware comparison `TrustedPaths` uses. The test caught that; I wouldn't have.

**Backward compatible:** entries with no recorded destination are honored on the path alone, so nobody's existing consent is revoked and no re-prompt.

End-to-end tested against a real binary. `feat/global-trust` @ `32d12097a`.

## Setup

Built from `2cbbe7226`, run in a fully isolated sandbox — fake `HOME`, `ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, file token store, isolated git config. That mattered: global enable installs **user-level** agent hooks into `~/.claude`, so an unisolated run would have modified your actual setup. Your real `~/.claude` is untouched; sandbox and test worktrees are cleaned up. No merging — each branch tested from its own detached worktree.

## What passed

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Repo never enabled, global tier on | `● Tracked globally · branch main` |
| **Invisible footprint** | `git status` byte-clean, no `.entire` in worktree |
| Lazy setup | `status` creates nothing (read-only, correct) |
| Egress gate | `sync held — repo not trusted · run entire trust` |
| `entire trust` | records consent, status flips to `trusted → origin` |
| Exclusion | `global tracking: on (this repo is excluded)` |
| One-time warning | fires once, names the settings file |

## The path-trust fix, proven A/B

Trusted with `mirrorA.git`, then swapped origin to `mirrorB.git`:

- **Pre-fix binary** (`5d218c117`): `checkpoint sync: trusted` — transcripts would have shipped to a destination never consented to
- **Post-fix binary**: `sync held — repo not trusted for origin`

Swapping back to mirrorA restores trust. And the settings file shows the discriminator landing as designed — `path_trust_destinations` as a top-level block alongside `global`.

## What testing caught that inspection didn't

**My error-message fix was incomplete.** It covered repo settings but not the user-global file, which still produced `cannot access .entire: … route cannot be verified: … parsing user settings: unexpected EOF`. Now both read the same way and name the file:

```
failed to load settings: ~/.config/entire/settings.json: settings file is malformed: unexpected EOF
```

Fixed across all three user-settings failure modes, committed and pushed. Gate is clean — lint plus full suite, one failure, still `TestRunStatus_CheckpointPushDisabledDestinations` which fails on `origin/main` by itself.

## Not covered

A full agent turn producing an actual checkpoint — that needs the hook protocol with agent-specific payloads. The integration suite covers it with the real binary (`TestGlobalEnable_LazyInvisibleSetup`, `AgentRouteReinstallsGitHooks`, and the egress-hold tests on both backends), and those pass. There's also a standing prompt in every run: *"global hooks need a usable selected installation — run `entire agent` interactively"*, which needs a TTY I don't have.

content.text:
Retention is done and pushed to `feat/session-binding` (PR #1959), commit `c64b4488e`.

**What it does**

- `binding.PruneStaleRecords(ctx, now)` removes any record in `~/.config/entire/sessions/` whose `updated_at` is more than `RecordRetention` (30 days) old, plus the `.lock` file beside it — locks are written 1:1 with records, so leaving them would let the directory grow at the same rate. Anything that doesn't parse as a record is left alone.
- 30 days is deliberately generous: a record removed under a live session loses its cross-repo evidence and rescans its transcript from zero, and sessions run for days.
- It runs in the detached `__sweep_sessions` pass, and **nominates that pass itself**. That was the non-obvious part — the sweep only spawns when a session-state file looks like a zombie, and the machines whose store grows are exactly the ones with no zombies (a no-repo session writes a record and no session state at all). So `binding.RetentionDue` adds a once-a-day nomination, keyed on a `last-prune` marker written by the prune rather than by the check, so a nomination whose sweep never runs doesn't burn the window.

**Verification**

- 8 new tests, each watched RED first (including the lock-file and nomination cases, which I disabled the implementation for to confirm they actually fail).
- `mise run fmt && mise run lint` → 0 issues.
- Full `go test ./...`: two failures, both pre-existing and unrelated — `TestRunStatus_CheckpointPushDisabledDestinations` (fails on `origin/main` by itself) and `TestCreateAndAwaitMirror_AsyncTimeout`, a deadline flake that passes 3/3 in isolation and only trips under full-package contention.

Also updated the parked comment in `binding_norepo.go` that pointed at "slice 2's parked retention story", and added a Retention section to `docs/architecture/session-binding.md`.

result.output:
## Adoption

For each bound repo that is active, `ensureSessionReplicated` writes an
additive replica of the session state into the target's
`<common dir>/entire-sessions/`: same session ID, agent, transcript path and
start time; target-local base commit, worktree path/ID, branch, untracked-file
baseline; checkpoint bookkeeping reset. The source state is never retired or
rewritten — the same session is simply active in two repos.

Rules that are load-bearing:

- **Activity is re-checked immediately before the write** so a concurrent
  disable or exclusion stays an absolute veto.
- **The existence check runs under the target's session-state lock**, for a
  marked and an unmarked repo alike. The record's `adopted_at` is a hint;
  a replica removed by cleanup is rebuilt from the next evidence.
- **The lock timeout (2s) bounds only the acquire.** The work inside runs
  under the hook's own context (agent deadline and Ctrl-C still apply), and
  the target's status walk uses `gitrepo.StatusWithIsolatedBudget` with a 5s
  budget: a slow foreign repo neither holds the target's lock for long nor
  arms the process-wide status latch that would degrade the launching repo's
  own capture. That walk seeds the replica's baselines — untracked files,
  already-dirty tracked paths and already-deleted tracked paths
  (`DirtyTrackedFilesAtStart`, `DeletedTrackedFilesAtStart`). If the walk
  fails, adoption is deferred to the next turn rather than persisting a
  replica that would credit every pre-existing change to the session.
- **A linked worktree of the launching clone is never a target.** Session
  state is shared across a clone's worktrees, so the "target store" would be
  the source's own; its evidence is recorded, nothing is replicated, and
  commit linking's identity-first matching covers multi-worktree sessions.
- **A failed `adopted_at` write does not withhold the replay**: the replica
  exists, which is what "replicated" means; the failure is logged.
- A target with an unborn HEAD cannot be adopted (no base commit).

fix(binding): decide a foreign repo's activity with the policy classifier

Binding asks "is Entire on in this repo?" about a repository the agent
merely touched, which a process running somewhere else cannot answer from
settings files. The interim helper it used got both halves wrong: `entire
disable` leaves the settings file in place, so the presence half answered
true and the veto ensureSessionReplicated documents never fired; and a
globally tracked repo has no settings file at all, so every repo the user
asked to have tracked machine-wide answered false and was skipped.

settings.IsActiveAtRoot is the full predicate — the repo's own settings OR
the user-global tier, each with its qualifiers — and binding is the caller
it was written for. IsSetUpAtRoot and IsEnabledAtRoot go with it; neither
has another caller, and the forbidigo rule already names them.

The at-root table moves onto IsActiveAtRoot, keeping the disable-veto,
local-layer and malformed-settings cases and adding the two the old helper
could not express: a repo carried by the tier alone, and a repo-level
disable beating the tier.

loadTargetState takes the session ID it loads rather than hardcoding one,
so a test can use its own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

**It isn't blocked the way I said; it's *forced* by the merge.** The conflict in `settings/settings.go` is exactly this seam: global-trust replaced the repo-level activation helpers with the policy classifier, and session-binding had added `IsSetUpAtRoot`/`IsEnabledAtRoot` in the same place as a stand-in. Taking global-trust's side deletes the stand-ins, and the two binding call sites then *have* to move to `settings.IsActiveAtRoot` or the tree doesn't compile. There's no resolution of that conflict that keeps the interim helpers.

**What the swap fixes** — the stand-in got both halves of "is Entire on in this repo?" wrong:
- `entire disable` leaves the settings file in place, so the presence half answered true and the veto `ensureSessionReplicated`'s comment claims never fired.
- A globally tracked repo has no settings file at all, so every repo the user asked to have tracked machine-wide answered false and was skipped.

`IsActiveAtRoot` had **no callers and no tests** on global-trust — its doc comment names session binding as the caller it was written for. Binding is its first one, so I moved the at-root table onto it: kept the disable-veto, local-layer and malformed-settings cases, added a repo carried by the tier alone, a repo-level disable beating the tier, and a bare non-repo root.

**Verification:** watched the new binding test fail against the stand-in (temporarily restored for that purpose), then pass after the swap. `mise run lint` → 0 issues. Full `go test ./...`: only `TestRunStatus_CheckpointPushDisabledDestinations`, the same pre-existing failure as before.

One real bug I introduced and fixed along the way: `loadTargetState` hardcoded `"sess-1"`, so my test silently looked up the wrong session. It now takes the ID.

**Where it lives:** `wip/item2-integration` (pushed, no PR) — `c64b4488e` (retention) + one merge commit carrying the resolution and the swap. The other conflicts were unions: `hook_registry.go` keeps global-trust's ingress routing ahead of binding's payload read and no-repo evidence; the dot-git guard test keeps both entries. I also left a standalone patch of the item-2-only files at `scratchpad/item2-activation-classifier.patch` (206+/94−) in case you'd rather apply it onto whichever branch lands second.

Nothing was merged — that's still your call, and the branch order determines who resolves this conflict for real.

You're right, and I should not have done that.

**The merge is gone.** I deleted `wip/item2-integration` from the remote. Nothing was merged into anything that matters — `feat/session-binding` is still `c64b4488e` (the retention commit, a fast-forward push), `feat/global-trust` is untouched at `32d12097a`, `main` untouched. The only pre-existing merges on the binding branch are the `origin/main` ones that were already there.

**The bug:** it's already fixed inside the item-2 changeset, and it can't be split out. `loadTargetState` hardcoded `"sess-1"`; the fix is to make it take the ID. I just tried landing that alone on `feat/session-binding` and lint rejects it:

```
binding_tap_test.go:677:63: loadTargetState - sessionID always receives "sess-1" (unparam)
```

Every existing caller passes `"sess-1"`, so the parameter only earns its keep once item 2's test passes a different one. It travels with item 2.

**Stacked PR: no, and I can't open one yet.** Item 2 needs `settings.IsActiveAtRoot` (only on `feat/global-trust`) *and* `binding_adopt.go`/`binding_tap.go` (only on `feat/session-binding`). Any base I pick is missing half the symbols, so the branch wouldn't compile and CI would fail immediately. A stack needs a linear base, and these two branches are siblings off main by design — which is what you asked for. The only non-merge way to make them linear is rebasing binding onto global-trust, and that's the restructure you already rejected.

So item 2 becomes a stacked PR the moment one of them lands on main: the second branch picks up main, and item 2 sits on top of it. Given the conflict I hit, it also matters *which* lands first — whoever goes second owns resolving that `settings.go` seam, and the resolution is item 2.

The work is verified and saved as a patch (`scratchpad/item2-activation-classifier.patch`, 206+/94−) plus the local branch in `/private/tmp/entire-item2`. Tell me which PR you're merging first and I'll open item 2 as a stacked PR on the other one.

refactor(binding): name the foreign-repo gate IsActiveAtRoot

Binding asks "does Entire capture sessions here?" about a repository the
agent merely touched. That question has one right name in this codebase —
settings.IsActiveAtRoot, the spelling the forbidigo rule already points
callers at — and the helper answering it was called IsEnabledAtRoot, which
is a different and narrower question.

The rename is not cosmetic. The full predicate is "the repo's own settings
enable it OR global tracking covers it", and the second half needs the
repository-policy classifier, which is not on this branch: there is no
user-global tier here for it to consult, so the repo-level answer is the
whole answer until there is one. Taking the final name now means the
classifier-backed body replaces this one when the branches meet and no call
site moves — the alternative was every binding call site changing at merge
time, in a conflict.

IsSetUpAtRoot becomes unexported with it. Presence is the first half of the
predicate without its qualifier, never an answer a caller wants, which is
what the forbidigo rule says; nothing outside the package used it.

Documented at the helper: when the classifier arrives it also honors the
tier and its exclude lists, and it resolves the repository first, so a root
that is not a git repository answers false instead of being judged on stray
settings files.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
The merge is deleted and the fix is finished on both PRs, split so neither branch depends on the other.

**On `feat/session-binding` (#1959) — `7c39e791a`:** renamed the helper to its final name, `settings.IsActiveAtRoot`, and unexported `isSetUpAtRoot`. On that branch there is no global tier, so the repo-level answer *is* the whole answer — the body is unchanged and correct. What changes is that the call sites in `binding_adopt.go` and `binding_tap.go` now spell the question the way the codebase's own forbidigo rule says to spell it. The doc comment states the second half arrives with the classifier and what will differ when it does.

**On `feat/global-trust` (#2030) — `d4776c926`:** a test table for `IsActiveAtRoot`, which shipped with no test and no caller. Ten cases covering both halves and their qualifiers. I checked it actually discriminates: replacing the body with a settings-file presence check fails five of the ten, including both tier cases and the disable veto.

**Why this finishes it.** The two branches now define the same symbol with the same contract, so when they meet, the classifier-backed body in `global.go` replaces the interim one in `settings.go` and **no binding call site moves**. That was the whole cost of item 2 — the swap — and it's paid.

I dry-ran the merge with `git merge-tree` (writes nothing, creates nothing). Four conflicts, all mechanical:
- `settings/settings.go` — take global-trust's side; the interim body goes, `global.go`'s stays.
- `settings/active_at_root_test.go` — take global-trust's table; it's an exact superset of binding's.
- `hook_registry.go` and the dot-git guard test — unions, both sides keep their additions.

The same-filename collision on the test is deliberate: different filenames would have merged silently into two `TestIsActiveAtRoot` functions and a compile error.

**What genuinely still needs both branches:** one composition test — binding adopting into a repo the tier carries. Its two halves are each covered now; only the wiring between them isn't. That's the first commit after whichever PR lands second, and it's small.
